calmness and quiet on the message it has for us.
In order rightly to understand the story which Jesus
narrates in our text, we must remember a custom which
existed in the country and at the time of Jesus. When a man
of means proposed to give a grand banquet, he first issued a
preliminary invitation, without specifying the day and the
hour of its taking place. Thus the guests were warned that
they should hold themselves in readiness for an occasion in
the near future. Then, when the day came, a second invita-
tion was issued: "The day is here; come, for everything is
prepared!"
In accordance with this custom, the rich man of whom
our story tells had invited many guests and of course they
had accepted his invitation; for who would want to miss such
a banquet? But they had accepted somewhat casually; for,
as we see, when the time came they were not ready. They did
not organize their time and business with a view to the fact
that shortly the host's messenger would come and invite
them for the particular day, but they went on with their
affairs and daily pursuits as though the final invitation to the
feast were not shortly to be expected; in fact they probably
forgot the invitation altogether. When therefore the messenger
comes, the attention of all of them is claimed by things which
for the moment seem more important than the banquet.
One has bought a field and must go out to consider how to
exploit it best; another has bought oxen and must go and
look after them; the third has married a wife and therefore
is prevented. The remainder who are not expressly men-
tioned have one thing or another which precludes their
coming. In short, none of those who were bidden have now
time to come; none comes to the banquet.

who will be glad to come." So he sends his messenger out
